name: Affirming a disjunct
aliases: affirming one disjunct; fallacy of the alternative syllogism; asserting an alternative; improper disjunctive syllogism; disjunctive syllogism, fallacy of
definition: From "P or Q" and P, concluding not-Q (treating an inclusive "or" as exclusive).
example: "He's either smart or hardworking. He's smart, so he isn't hardworking."
not_fallacious_when: When the disjunction is genuinely exclusive (e.g. "the switch is on or off").

name: Affirming the consequent
aliases: fallacy of the consequent (Aristotle); converse error; affirmation of the consequent
definition: From "if P then Q" and Q, concluding P.
example: "If she's the thief, her prints are on the safe. Her prints are on the safe. So she's the thief."
not_fallacious_when: As abductive inference to the best explanation once rival explanations are ruled out, or when the conditional is really a biconditional; then it is defeasible evidence, not proof.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 167b1 (consequent); ARI-RH II.24 (line 6, consequence); WHA (logical); MIL V.vi; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-RH WHA MIL WIK IEP LF FF

name: Commutation of conditionals
aliases: converting a conditional; conversion of a conditional
definition: From "if P then Q", concluding "if Q then P".
example: "If it's a cat it has fur, so if it has fur it's a cat."
not_fallacious_when: When there is independent evidence that the relation runs both ways (a biconditional).

name: Denying a conjunct
definition: From "not both P and Q" and not-P, concluding Q.
example: "You can't be both at home and at work. You're not at work, so you're at home."
not_fallacious_when: Valid only if the premise is really "exactly one of P, Q".

name: Denying the antecedent
aliases: inverse error; denial of the antecedent
definition: From "if P then Q" and not-P, concluding not-Q.
example: "If it's a dog it's a mammal. It's not a dog. So it's not a mammal."
not_fallacious_when: When "if" is meant as "only if" in context (e.g. "If you finish your homework you can go out" often implies the converse); recognising the conversational implicature is legitimate.
primary_sources: MIL V.vi; WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Improper transposition
aliases: negating antecedent and consequent; transposition, improper
definition: From "if P then Q", concluding "if not-P then not-Q" (instead of the valid "if not-Q then not-P").
example: "If it rains the ground gets wet; so if it doesn't rain the ground stays dry."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid as a form; sometimes the conclusion is true for other reasons.

name: Invalid reasoning (generic formal fallacy)
aliases: formal fallacy; non sequitur (formal sense); logical fallacy (narrow sense)
definition: Any argument whose form does not guarantee its conclusion even if the premises are true.
example: "Some politicians lie; some liars are rich; so some politicians are rich."
not_fallacious_when: Invalid by deductive standards does not mean worthless: much good reasoning is inductive or defeasible and should be judged by those standards (Massey's asymmetry thesis warns that invalidity is hard to prove).
primary_sources: SEP §3.2 (Massey 1981; Finocchiaro); IEP "Formal Fallacy"; LF; FF

name: Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise
definition: A syllogism draws an affirmative conclusion though a premise is negative.
example: "No reptiles have fur; all snakes are reptiles; so all snakes have fur."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid as a syllogism.

name: Exclusive premises
aliases: two negative premises; two negative premisses; exclusive premisses
definition: A syllogism with two negative premises; nothing follows.
example: "No fish are mammals; no birds are fish; so no birds are mammals."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid as a syllogism.

name: Four terms
definition: A syllogism that actually uses four terms, usually because one word shifts meaning.
example: "Nothing is better than God; a sandwich is better than nothing; so a sandwich is better than God."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid; often a disguised equivocation, so diagnose the shifting term.
primary_sources: MIL V.vi; WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Illicit contraposition
definition: Contraposing an E or I proposition, which is invalid.
example: "Some dogs are not pets, so some non-pets are not non-dogs" (misapplied forms).
not_fallacious_when: Contraposition is valid for A and O propositions.

name: Illicit conversion
aliases: false conversion; conversion of A or O propositions; inductive conversion (IEP, for "most/many")
definition: Swapping subject and predicate where that is not allowed: from "All S are P" to "All P are S" (or "most" to "most").
example: "Most NBA players are tall, so most tall people are NBA players."
not_fallacious_when: Conversion is valid for E ("No S are P") and I ("Some S are P") propositions.
primary_sources: MIL V.vi (conversion of universal affirmatives and particular negatives); SEP §2.8; IEP; LF; FF

name: Illicit major
aliases: illicit process of the major; illicit process (major)
definition: The major term covers its whole class in the conclusion but not in the premise.
example: "All dogs are animals; no cats are dogs; so no cats are animals."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid as a syllogism.

name: Illicit minor
definition: The minor term covers its whole class in the conclusion but not in the premise.
example: "All cats are mammals; all cats are animals; so all animals are mammals."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid as a syllogism.

name: Negative conclusion from affirmative premises
definition: A syllogism draws a negative conclusion from only affirmative premises.
example: "All A are B; all B are C; so some A are not C."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid as a syllogism.

name: Undistributed middle
aliases: maldistributed middle; fallacy of the undistributed middle
definition: In a syllogism, the middle term never covers its whole class, so the two other terms may not be linked.
example: "All communists oppose the bill; she opposes the bill; so she's a communist."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid; the same evidence can support a weak probabilistic inference, labelled as such.
primary_sources: WHA (purely logical); MIL V.vi; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: WHA MIL WIK IEP LF FF

name: Existential fallacy
aliases: existential assumption, fallacy of; existential import fallacy
definition: Drawing a "some" conclusion from "all" premises that may be about nothing.
example: "All unicorns have horns, so some unicorns have horns."
not_fallacious_when: Valid if one adds (or the context guarantees) that the class is non-empty, as Aristotelian logic usually assumed.

name: Masked man fallacy
aliases: illicit substitution of identicals; intensional fallacy; hooded man (Eubulides); epistemic substitution failure
definition: Substituting co-referring names inside belief, knowledge or modal contexts where the substitution can change truth.
example: "I know my father; I don't know the masked man; so the masked man isn't my father."
not_fallacious_when: Substitution is fine in purely extensional contexts ("Cicero is Roman" to "Tully is Roman").

name: Modal scope fallacy
aliases: modal fallacy; misconditionalization; fallacy of necessity (necessitas consequentiae vs. consequentis)
definition: Moving "necessarily" from a whole conditional onto its consequent.
example: "Necessarily, if God foreknows I'll sin, I'll sin; God foreknows it; so I necessarily sin."
not_fallacious_when: Correct when the consequent really is necessary on independent grounds.

name: Quantifier shift
aliases: quantifier-shift fallacy; illicit quantifier shift; fallacy of every and all; every-and-all
definition: Swapping "for every x there is some y" into "there is some y for every x".
example: "Everything has a cause, so there is one cause of everything."
not_fallacious_when: Never valid by form; the stronger claim may be argued separately.

name: Some are / some are not
definition: Inferring "some S are not P" from "some S are P" (or vice versa).
example: "Some students passed, so some students failed."
not_fallacious_when: As a conversational implicature ("some" often suggests "not all") it is a reasonable guess, not a deduction.

name: Appeal to probability
definition: Treating something as true or certain because it is possible or probable.
example: "Hackers could have broken in, so they did."
not_fallacious_when: In risk management, planning for likely or even possible harms is prudent; that is a practical, not factual, conclusion.
primary_sources: FIS (fallacy of the possible proof; via secondary sources); WIK; LF

name: Base rate fallacy
aliases: base rate neglect; neglecting base rates
definition: Judging probability from case-specific evidence while ignoring how common the thing is overall.
example: "The test is 99% accurate and he tested positive, so he almost certainly has the rare disease."
not_fallacious_when: Ignoring base rates is reasonable only when they are unknown or genuinely irrelevant to the reference class.
primary_sources: Kahneman & Tversky 1973 (Psych. Review 80); Bar-Hillel 1980; WIK; LF; FF

name: Conjunction fallacy
definition: Judging "A and B" more probable than A alone.
example: "Linda is more likely a feminist bank teller than a bank teller."
not_fallacious_when: Not a fallacy if the question is read as "which description fits better" (representativeness), a point critics of the Linda studies have pressed.
primary_sources: Tversky & Kahneman 1983 (Psych. Review 90); WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Defense attorney's fallacy
definition: Dismissing incriminating statistical evidence because many others in a large population would also match, ignoring other evidence that narrows the pool.
example: "In a city of 10 million, 10 people match this DNA, so the match only gives a 1-in-10 chance of guilt."
not_fallacious_when: Correct only if there truly is no other evidence linking the defendant.

name: Disjunction fallacy
definition: Judging "A or B" less probable than A alone.
example: "It's less likely that it rains or snows tomorrow than that it rains."
not_fallacious_when: Never correct by probability calculus.

name: Double counting
definition: Counting the same event or evidence more than once, inflating probabilities or support.
example: Citing three news reports that all repeat a single original source as three confirmations.
not_fallacious_when: Repeated independent observations legitimately add support.

name: Gambler's fallacy
aliases: Monte Carlo fallacy; maturity of chances; fallacy of the maturity of chances
definition: Thinking independent random outcomes "even out", so a streak makes the opposite more likely.
example: "Red came up six times; black is due."
not_fallacious_when: If the process is not independent (e.g. drawing cards without replacement), past outcomes do change the odds.

name: Hot hand fallacy
definition: Believing a streak of successes makes the next success more likely in a random process.
example: "He's hit five in a row; give him the ball."
not_fallacious_when: Contested: Miller & Sanjurjo (2018, Econometrica 86) found a bias in the original analysis and evidence of a real, modest hot hand in basketball shooting; streaks can reflect real changes in skill or conditions.
primary_sources: Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky 1985 (Cognitive Psychology 17); LF; FF

name: Independence fallacy
definition: Multiplying probabilities of events as if independent when they are linked.
example: An expert squares the chance of one cot death to get the chance of two in one family, ignoring shared genetic and environmental factors.
not_fallacious_when: Multiplication is correct when independence is established.

name: Inverse gambler's fallacy
definition: Inferring from one improbable outcome that the process must have been run many times before.
example: "Double six on the first roll? They must have been rolling for a while."
not_fallacious_when: Many-trials explanations can be legitimate when we have independent selection-effect reasons (observer selection).

name: Lottery fallacy
definition: Treating the occurrence of a specific improbable outcome as remarkable when some such outcome was bound to happen.
example: "The odds of her winning were a million to one, so it must be rigged."
not_fallacious_when: Improbability matters when the outcome was specified in advance or matches an independent pattern.

name: Ludic fallacy
definition: Treating messy real-world uncertainty as if it followed the clean odds of a game or model.
example: "Our model says this crash is a 25-sigma event, so it won't happen again."
not_fallacious_when: Models are legitimate approximations when their assumptions are checked against the domain.
primary_sources: Taleb, The Black Swan (2007); WIK; LF

name: Prosecutor's fallacy
aliases: transposed conditional; inverse probability fallacy; fallacy of the inverted conditional
definition: Confusing P(evidence given innocence) with P(innocence given evidence).
example: "Only 1 in a million would match this DNA, so there's a 1 in a million chance he's innocent."
not_fallacious_when: None as an inference; the figures can be combined correctly using base rates (Bayes).
primary_sources: Thompson & Schumann 1987 (Law & Human Behavior 11); WIK; IEP

name: Accusation-scarer's device
definition: Deterring accusations by warning that a failed accusation will disgrace the accuser.
example: "If you can't prove this charge, you'll be ruined."
not_fallacious_when: False accusations are harmful; standards for making charges are legitimate.

name: Ad fidentia
definition: Attacking the person's self-confidence instead of their argument.
example: "You're not even sure of yourself; why should we listen?"
not_fallacious_when: Confidence levels can be relevant if the person is reporting a perception or memory.

name: Ad hominem (abusive)
aliases: argumentum ad hominem; personal attack; abusive ad hominem; smear tactic; against the person; name calling; argumentum ad personam (Schopenhauer); imputation of bad character (Bentham)
definition: Rejecting a claim by attacking the speaker's character instead of the argument.
example: "His theory of justice is worthless; he's a drunk."
not_fallacious_when: When the speaker's credibility is itself the issue (testimony, eyewitness reliability, expert trustworthiness). Walton treats ad hominem as a defeasible scheme with critical questions; many uses are fair.
primary_sources: SCH 38 (ad personam); BEN II.1.2 (vituperative personalities); WAL (Ad Hominem Arguments, 1998); SEP §1, §2.4; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: BEN SCH WAL SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Anti-rational fallacy
aliases: anti-rational fallacies (Bentham); "good in theory, bad in practice"; "utopian"; "too good to be practicable"; abuse of "speculative"/"theoretical"
definition: Dismissing an argument as "theoretical" or "utopian" without showing where it fails in practice.
example: "That's fine in theory but it won't work in practice."
not_fallacious_when: Theories can omit real practical constraints; name them. Schopenhauer: what is right in theory must work in practice, else the theory is wrong (stratagem 33).

name: Appeal to authority (illegitimate)
aliases: argumentum ad verecundiam; appeal to unqualified authority; appeal to false authority; argument from false authority; misleading appeal to authority; single authority; blind authority fallacy; anonymous authority; appeal to celebrity; self-assumed authority (Bentham); sophism of authority (Port-Royal)
definition: Accepting a claim because someone of status asserts it when their authority is irrelevant, unqualified, unnamed, contested or unexamined.
example: "A famous actor says this supplement cures anxiety."
not_fallacious_when: Deferring to genuine experts within their field is rational, especially when experts agree and their claim is backed by evidence (Walton's six critical questions; Bentham's conditions for reliable authority).
primary_sources: LOC IV.xvii.19; PR III.xx.6–7; BEN I.1, I.5; SCH 30; WAL (Appeal to Expert Opinion, 1997); SEP §1, §2.4; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: LOC PR BEN SCH WAL SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Appeal to closure
definition: Accepting an explanation because people want the matter settled.
example: "We need to move on; let's accept this explanation."
not_fallacious_when: Decisions often must be made under uncertainty; accept provisionally and say so.

name: Appeal to common folk
definition: Seeking agreement by presenting oneself as an ordinary person "just like you."
example: "I'm just a regular guy like you, and I know this tax is wrong."
not_fallacious_when: Shared experience can supply relevant testimony.

name: Appeal to common sense
definition: Claiming a conclusion is "just common sense" when it is disputed.
example: "It's common sense that punishment deters crime."
not_fallacious_when: Common sense is a reasonable default in everyday matters and a check on wild theories.

name: Appeal to consequences
aliases: argumentum ad consequentiam; appeal to consequence; consequence
definition: Judging a factual claim true or false by whether its consequences are pleasant.
example: "There can't be an afterlife, because that would be terrifying."
not_fallacious_when: For practical conclusions (what to do or adopt), consequences are central and legitimate reasons.

name: Appeal to desperation
definition: Arguing your proposal is right because something must be done and it is something.
example: "We must do something; this is something; so we must do this."
not_fallacious_when: Urgency is a real reason to act; it doesn't pick which action.

name: Appeal to emotion
aliases: argumentum ad passiones; emotional appeal; irrelevant emotional appeal; appeal to anger
definition: Getting a claim accepted by arousing feelings rather than giving reasons that bear on it.
example: "Think of the children! Vote yes."
not_fallacious_when: Emotions can track real values; in deciding what to do, fitting emotions (compassion, fear of real danger) are relevant. Aristotle counts pathos as a genuine mode of proof (Rhetoric I.2).
primary_sources: ARI-RH I.2 (pathos as proof); ARI-RH II.24 (line 3); WIK; LF; FF

name: Appeal to equality
definition: Treating a claim as settled by an appeal to "equality" without saying what must be equal or why.
example: "Everyone deserves equal results, so grade everyone the same."
not_fallacious_when: Equality claims are central in ethics when the relevant respect of equality is specified and argued.

name: Appeal to extremes
definition: Turning a reasonable claim into an absurd one by pushing it to extremes.
example: "If we raise the minimum wage, why not $1,000 an hour?"
not_fallacious_when: Testing a principle at its limits is legitimate (it's how reductio works) if the principle really implies the extreme.

name: Appeal to faith
definition: Asking for acceptance on faith in place of reasons, especially when reasons point the other way.
example: "You just have to believe it."
not_fallacious_when: Some traditions argue faith is a distinct, legitimate mode of assent; that is a substantive philosophical claim to be argued.

name: Appeal to fear
aliases: argumentum ad metum; scare tactic; fear appeal; hobgoblin argument ("No innovation!", Bentham); just in case fallacy
definition: Using fear, not evidence, to get a claim accepted.
example: "If you vote for him, the country will fall into chaos."
not_fallacious_when: Warning of a real and probable danger is a good practical argument.
primary_sources: BEN II.2 (hobgoblin, ad metum); WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Appeal to flattery
definition: Winning agreement through praise of the listener instead of reasons.
example: "A smart person like you can surely see this is the right investment."
not_fallacious_when: Sincere praise can be fine; it just isn't evidence.

name: Appeal to force
aliases: argumentum ad baculum; appeal to the stick; appeal to threat; proof by intimidation
definition: Making acceptance a matter of threats rather than reasons.
example: "Agree with the plan or you'll be looking for a new job."
not_fallacious_when: Threats are real reasons for action (laws with sanctions, negotiation), just not evidence that a claim is true. Pragma-dialectics treats it as a breach of the freedom rule.
primary_sources: PD (freedom rule); SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: PD SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Appeal to heaven
aliases: appeal to divine will; deus vult
definition: Claiming a conclusion must be accepted because it is God's will.
example: "God wants us to build this wall."
not_fallacious_when: Within a shared theological framework, appeals to accepted revelation are internal reasons.

name: Appeal to intuition
definition: Accepting or rejecting an argument on an unarticulated gut feeling.
example: "I just feel it's wrong; I don't need reasons."
not_fallacious_when: Intuitions serve as data in philosophy (reflective equilibrium) and experts' intuitions can be reliable; they should be stated and weighed.

name: Appeal to loyalty
definition: Asking people to accept a claim out of loyalty to a group or person.
example: "A true member wouldn't question the leadership's numbers."
not_fallacious_when: Loyalty is a real value in deciding how to act; it isn't evidence of truth.

name: Appeal to nature
definition: Treating "natural" as good (or "unnatural" as bad) without further argument.
example: "It's herbal, so it's safe."
not_fallacious_when: "Natural" can sometimes be shorthand for a real property (well-tested, low-processed); argue that property directly.

name: Appeal to normality
definition: Treating what is normal or typical as therefore good, and the abnormal as bad.
example: "It's not normal to be single at 40, so something's wrong."
not_fallacious_when: Statistical normality can signal safety or fit in some practical contexts.

name: Appeal to novelty
aliases: argumentum ad novitatem; appeal to modernity
definition: Treating something as better simply because it's new.
example: "It's the latest version, so it must be better."
not_fallacious_when: In fast-improving fields, newer often is better on average; a presumption, not a proof.

name: Appeal to pity
definition: Seeking acceptance by evoking sympathy rather than reasons.
example: "Professor, I deserve an A; I've had a terrible semester."
not_fallacious_when: Suffering is relevant when the question is about mercy, aid or sentencing.

name: Appeal to popularity
aliases: argumentum ad populum; appeal to the people; appeal to common belief; appeal to common practice; consensus gentium; authority of the many; argument by consensus; appeal to the masses; appeal to the mob; mob appeal; appeal to the gallery; ad numerum; common belief
definition: Treating wide acceptance as proof that a claim is true or good.
example: "Millions of people believe in astrology, so there must be something to it."
not_fallacious_when: In matters of convention (word meanings, etiquette, which side of the road) popularity is constitutive; independent agreement of many can be weak evidence.

name: Appeal to pride
aliases: argumentum ad superbiam; appeal to snobbery
definition: Persuading by appealing to the listener's pride or sense of status.
example: "Only discerning people appreciate this wine."
not_fallacious_when: Appeals to self-respect can be motivationally fair when the action is independently justified.

name: Appeal to ridicule
aliases: appeal to mockery; horse laugh; reductio ad ridiculum
definition: Mocking a position instead of answering it.
example: "Evolution? So your grandfather was a monkey?"
not_fallacious_when: Satire can fairly expose a real absurdity after it has been shown.

name: Appeal to self-evident truth
definition: Declaring something self-evident when it is disputed, to avoid arguing for it.
example: "It's self-evident that markets are always efficient."
not_fallacious_when: Genuine axioms and definitions are starting points (Spinoza's axioms; pragma-dialectical starting points) if actually shared.

name: Appeal to spite
aliases: appeal to hatred; appeal to envy; argumentum ad odium (Bentham's class); argumentum ad invidiam
definition: Using ill will toward someone as a reason to accept or reject a claim.
example: "Support the tax; those snobs deserve to pay."
not_fallacious_when: Resentment can point to a real injustice that then needs argument.
primary_sources: BEN II.1 (ad odium); WIK; LF; FF

name: Appeal to stupidity
definition: Urging an audience to devalue reason, expertise or discussion.
example: "You don't need fancy studies; just trust your gut like normal people."
not_fallacious_when: Scepticism about overconfident experts can be reasonable when grounded.

name: Appeal to the law
definition: Treating what is legal as therefore right, or illegal as therefore wrong.
example: "It's legal, so there's nothing wrong with it."
not_fallacious_when: Law often reflects considered moral judgments and the value of the rule of law is itself a reason.

name: Appeal to the moon
aliases: "if we can put a man on the moon"
definition: Arguing that because one hard thing was achieved, an unrelated hard thing must be achievable.
example: "If we can put a man on the moon, we can cure the common cold."
not_fallacious_when: An analogy of difficulty can be fair if the challenges are actually similar.

name: Appeal to the stone
aliases: argumentum ad lapidem; pooh-pooh; dismissal without argument
definition: Dismissing a claim as absurd without showing why.
example: "That's obviously ridiculous" (said in reply to a sceptical argument).
not_fallacious_when: Appeals to plain, shared certainty (Moore-style) carry some weight, and triage of crank claims is often reasonable.
primary_sources: Named after Samuel Johnson's stone-kick reply to Berkeley (Boswell, Life of Johnson, 1791); WIK

name: Appeal to tradition
aliases: argumentum ad antiquitatem; wisdom of our ancestors (Bentham's "Chinese argument"); appeal to past practice; traditional wisdom; argument from age; past practice
definition: Treating long standing as proof that something is true or right.
example: "We've always done it this way."
not_fallacious_when: Long-lived practices may encode tested knowledge (a presumption, as in "Chesterton's fence"); fallacious only when age replaces examination.

name: Appeal to trust
definition: Assuming whatever a trusted source says is true (or untrusted source false).
example: "It was in that paper, so it's true."
not_fallacious_when: Trust in reliable sources is rational as a default; it should yield to specific contrary evidence.

name: Appeal to wealth or poverty
aliases: argumentum ad crumenam; argument to the purse; appeal to money; argumentum ad lazarum; appeal to poverty
definition: Judging a claim by the wealth or poverty of its proponent.
example: "He's a billionaire, so his economic advice must be right."
not_fallacious_when: Wealth or poverty can be relevant evidence of a track record or of lived experience.

name: Bandwagon fallacy
aliases: bandwagon; peer pressure; appeal to trend
definition: Urging belief or action because more and more people are adopting it.
example: "Everyone's switching to this app; you should too."
not_fallacious_when: Network effects make popularity a real practical reason (a phone network everyone uses).

name: Bulverism
definition: Assuming a view is wrong and explaining why the person holds it, instead of showing it is wrong.
example: "You only believe in free markets because you're rich."
not_fallacious_when: Once an error is shown independently, explaining its psychological origin is fair.
primary_sources: C. S. Lewis, "Bulverism" (1941 essay; repr. in God in the Dock); WIK; LF

name: Chronological snobbery
definition: Rejecting an idea because it belongs to an earlier, supposedly discredited era.
example: "People believed that in the Middle Ages, so it's obviously wrong."
not_fallacious_when: An older view may have been specifically refuted; then cite the refutation.
primary_sources: C. S. Lewis, Surprised by Joy (1955), ch. 13; WIK

name: Circumstantial ad hominem
aliases: appeal to motive; faulty motives; vested interest; imputation of bad motive; imputation of bad design (Bentham)
definition: Dismissing a claim because the speaker's situation or interests might motivate it.
example: "Of course the oil executive says the pipeline is safe."
not_fallacious_when: An interest is a good reason to check the evidence harder, and decisive when we rely only on the person's word.
primary_sources: BEN II.1.1, II.1.3; SEP §2.4; WIK; IEP

name: Confusing an explanation with an excuse
definition: Treating an explanation of something as if it justified it (or rejecting an explanation because it seems to excuse).
example: "You're explaining why terrorists act; so you're defending them."
not_fallacious_when: Some explanations do mitigate responsibility; say so.

name: Courtier's reply
definition: Dismissing a critic because they haven't studied the field's (often unspecified) sophisticated literature.
example: "You can't criticise astrology until you've read the great astrologers."
not_fallacious_when: Fair when the critic demonstrably misunderstands a specific technical point.
primary_sources: P. Z. Myers, Pharyngula blog (2006) (coined); WIK

name: Fallacy of relative privation
aliases: relative privation; appeal to worse problems; not as bad as; false consolation (Bentham)
definition: Dismissing a problem because worse problems exist elsewhere.
example: "Why complain about potholes when people are starving?"
not_fallacious_when: Prioritizing scarce resources by severity is legitimate in planning.
primary_sources: BEN III.2 (false consolation, ad quietem); WIK; LF

name: Gadarene swine fallacy
definition: Assuming that the person out of step with the group must be the one who is wrong.
example: "Everyone else agrees; you must be mistaken."
not_fallacious_when: Majority judgment is often a reasonable default (wisdom of crowds) when judgments are independent.

name: Galileo gambit
definition: Claiming that because an idea is ridiculed or opposed, it must be true (as Galileo's was).
example: "They laughed at Galileo, and they laugh at me."
not_fallacious_when: Persecution can be evidence of an establishment's motives; the idea still needs evidence.

name: Genetic fallacy
definition: Judging a claim by where it came from instead of on its merits.
example: "That idea came from a cult leader, so it's false."
not_fallacious_when: Origin bears on the reliability of testimony and sources, and debunking explanations can be strong (Boudry et al. 2015).
primary_sources: Cohen & Nagel, An Introduction to Logic and Scientific Method (1934) (early use); WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Group think fallacy
definition: Substituting pride in group membership for reasons supporting the group's view.
example: "If that's what our team thinks, that's good enough for me."
not_fallacious_when: Trusting a group with a strong track record is a form of reasonable deference.

name: Guilt by association
aliases: association fallacy; bad company fallacy; company that you keep fallacy; honor by association; noscitur ex sociis (Bentham); fallacy of opposition; imputation of suspicious connections; identity of denomination (noscitur ex cognominibus, Bentham)
definition: Judging a claim or person by the company they keep or a label they share rather than on the merits.
example: "That policy is supported by extremists, so it must be bad."
not_fallacious_when: Associations can be evidence about a person's likely views or about risk (base rates), and membership can imply endorsement.
primary_sources: BEN II.1.5–6; WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Identity fallacy
definition: Judging an argument by the arguer's social identity (class, gender, ethnicity, etc.).
example: "You're a man, so your view on this policy doesn't count."
not_fallacious_when: Lived experience can be relevant testimony or evidence about a situation.

name: Irrelevant conclusion
aliases: ignoratio elenchi; missing the point; beside the point; irrelevant thesis; irrelevant reason
definition: An argument that may be good in itself but proves something other than what is at issue.
example: "The defendant is a devoted father, so he couldn't have committed fraud."
not_fallacious_when: Proving a related conclusion is fine if it is acknowledged as different.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 167a21; WHA (material: irrelevant conclusion); MIL V.vii; SEP §2.1, §2.7; WIK; IEP; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE WHA MIL SEP WIK IEP FF

name: Lack of proportion
aliases: exaggeration; making a mountain out of a molehill; amplification (deinosis, Aristotle)
definition: Exaggerating or downplaying a crucial point so its weight is misjudged.
example: "One tourist was mugged, so the whole country is lawless."
not_fallacious_when: Emphasis is legitimate when the weight given matches the evidence.

name: No-precedent argument
definition: Rejecting a proposal only because it has never been done before.
example: "No parliament has ever done this, so we shouldn't."
not_fallacious_when: Lack of precedent signals untested risks and may justify caution or trials.

name: Notable effort
definition: Treating the effort spent on something as a reason to accept its conclusion.
example: "He worked on this theory for 20 years, so it must be right."
not_fallacious_when: Effort can correlate with thoroughness; check the work itself.

name: Nutpicking
definition: Holding up an opposing group's most extreme or foolish member as if typical.
example: "Here's a video of one protester saying something absurd; that's what they all think."
not_fallacious_when: Fringe statements matter if shown to be representative or influential.

name: Official malefactor's screen
aliases: "Attack us, you attack Government" (Bentham, ad metum)
definition: Defending officials by treating criticism of them as an attack on government itself.
example: "Questioning this minister undermines the state."
not_fallacious_when: Some attacks on officials really are aimed at the institution; show it.

name: Opposer-general's justification
aliases: "Not measures but men" / "Not men but measures" (Bentham, ad invidiam)
definition: Opposing everything an opponent proposes because of who they are (or claiming principle while doing so).
example: "Whatever the government proposes, we oppose."
not_fallacious_when: Opposition parties may rightly scrutinize; blanket opposition is not argument.

name: Paradoxical assertion
definition: Discrediting a principle by asserting the paradox that it is dangerous or useless (e.g. "the principle of utility is dangerous").
example: "Simplifying the law would be mischievous."
not_fallacious_when: Surprising claims can be true and should be argued.

name: Partiality-preacher's argument
aliases: "From the abuse, argue not against the use" (Bentham)
definition: Defending an institution by condemning its abuses in general terms while blocking any specific remedy.
example: "Yes, there are abuses, but don't touch the system."
not_fallacious_when: Abuses can be separable from use, but then propose remedies for them.

name: Poisoning the well
definition: Discrediting a source in advance so anything they say is dismissed.
example: "Before my opponent speaks, remember he's a paid lobbyist."
not_fallacious_when: Warning an audience about a documented record of fabrication is legitimate.
primary_sources: Phrase associated with J. H. Newman's reply to Kingsley (Apologia, 1864); WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Popular corruption
definition: Arguing reform is pointless because the people are too corrupt to deserve or use it.
example: "The voters are too ignorant to be trusted with this power."
not_fallacious_when: Concerns about institutional capacity are legitimate when evidenced.

name: Positive ad hominem
aliases: laudatory personalities (Bentham, ad amicitiam); appeal to accomplishment; argument from good character
definition: Defending a claim or measure by praising the character or achievements of those who back it.
example: "She won a Nobel Prize in physics, so her diet book is right."
not_fallacious_when: Character and track record matter when we must rely on someone's judgment or discretion.

name: Pragmatic fallacy
definition: Claiming something is true because believing it worked or was beneficial for someone.
example: "Wearing my lucky socks works; I've won since I started."
not_fallacious_when: Pragmatist theories of truth exist; within them, usefulness is argued as a criterion, not assumed.

name: Red herring
aliases: smokescreen; clouding the issue; distraction; artful diversion (Bentham); diversion (Schopenhauer)
definition: Introducing an irrelevant topic to pull attention away from the issue.
example: "Why worry about pollution when unemployment is so high?"
not_fallacious_when: Raising a genuinely more urgent related issue is fair if openly framed as a change of topic.
primary_sources: BEN III.5; SCH 18; SCH 29; IEP; LF; FF

name: Reductio ad Hitlerum
aliases: Hitler card; argumentum ad Nazium; playing the Nazi card
definition: Discrediting a view because Hitler or the Nazis held it.
example: "Hitler was a vegetarian, so vegetarianism is suspect."
not_fallacious_when: Fair if the view under discussion is substantially the same as a Nazi policy whose wrongness is the very point.
primary_sources: Strauss, Natural Right and History (1953) (coined); LF; FF

name: Righteousness fallacy
definition: Assuming that because someone's intentions are good, their facts or arguments are right.
example: "She means well, so her statistics must be accurate."
not_fallacious_when: Intentions bear on blame and trust, not truth.

name: Rights to ought fallacy
definition: Treating having a right to do something as showing one ought to do it.
example: "I have a right to say it, so it's right to say it."
not_fallacious_when: Rights do establish permissions; whether to exercise them is a further question.

name: Scapegoating
definition: Unfairly blaming a person or group for a problem.
example: "The economy is bad because of immigrants."
not_fallacious_when: Assigning blame to the actually responsible party is legitimate.

name: Self-trumpeter's fallacy
definition: Officials citing their own professed integrity or good intentions as proof their conduct needs no scrutiny.
example: "I have served with honour for 30 years; this inquiry is an insult."
not_fallacious_when: A track record is evidence, but not a substitute for checking the specific conduct.

name: Statement of conversion
definition: Accepting a claim because someone tells how they were converted to it.
example: "I used to be a sceptic like you, but now I believe."
not_fallacious_when: A conversion story may convey the reasons that persuaded someone; evaluate those reasons.

name: Straw man
aliases: strawman; refutation by caricature; caricaturization; misrepresentation; extension (Schopenhauer)
definition: Attacking a distorted or weakened version of the opponent's position.
example: "She wants more bike lanes; so she wants to ban cars."
not_fallacious_when: Simplifying for exposition is fine if acknowledged; testing the real commitments of a view by reductio is legitimate. Pragma-dialectics: violates the standpoint rule.
primary_sources: PR III.xix.1; SCH 1; PD (standpoint rule); SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: PR SCH PD SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Style over substance
aliases: sophism of manner (Port-Royal); argument by personal charm; argument by fast talking; rhyme-as-reason
definition: Letting the elegance, fluency or charm of a presentation stand in for the merit of the case.
example: "He spoke so confidently and smoothly; he must be right."
not_fallacious_when: Clear presentation is a virtue; it helps understanding without proving anything.

name: Subjectivist fallacy
aliases: relativist fallacy; "true for you but not for me"
definition: Rejecting a claim on the grounds that truth is relative to the person.
example: "That may be true for you, but it isn't for me."
not_fallacious_when: Some claims really are perspective-relative (taste, some value judgments); then say so and why.

name: The end justifies the means
definition: Defending wrongful means by appeal to a good end, without weighing the means.
example: "We had to suppress the press to save democracy."
not_fallacious_when: Consequentialist ethics does weigh means by outcomes; it must count the means' costs too.

name: The quietist ("No complaint")
aliases: no complaint argument; quietist (Bentham, ad quietem)
definition: Claiming a grievance is unreal because few or none have complained.
example: "Nobody has complained about the rules, so they must be fair."
not_fallacious_when: Absence of complaints is weak evidence of satisfaction where complaining is easy and safe.

name: Time the innovator-general
definition: Arguing change is inevitable or good merely because times change.
example: "Times have changed; the law must change."
not_fallacious_when: Changed conditions are a real reason to revisit rules if specified.

name: Tone policing
definition: Dismissing a message because of its emotional tone rather than its content.
example: "I'd listen if you weren't so angry."
not_fallacious_when: Tone can matter to whether a discussion can continue (civility norms), but not to whether the claim is true.

name: Traitorous critic fallacy
aliases: ergo decedo; "love it or leave it"
definition: Answering criticism by saying the critic should leave the group, implying disloyalty.
example: "If you hate this country so much, move somewhere else."
not_fallacious_when: Questions about a critic's goals can be fair when evidence shows bad faith.

name: Tu quoque
aliases: you too; appeal to hypocrisy; whataboutism (related); imputation of inconsistency (Bentham)
definition: Rejecting a criticism because the critic does the same thing.
example: "You say I shouldn't smoke, but you smoke."
not_fallacious_when: Hypocrisy can be evidence the critic doesn't believe their own claim or lacks standing to blame; inconsistency is a fair challenge to someone's commitments.

name: Two wrongs make a right
definition: Justifying a wrong by pointing to another wrong.
example: "They cheated last year, so it's fine for us to cheat now."
not_fallacious_when: Proportionate retaliation or reciprocity can sometimes be argued on independent grounds (e.g. legal self-defence).

name: Wishful thinking
definition: Believing something because you want it to be true.
example: "The test results must be fine; I don't want to be sick."
not_fallacious_when: Hope can be a reasonable motive for action under uncertainty; it isn't evidence.

name: Accent
aliases: fallacy of accent; accentus; misleading accent; prosody
definition: Changing meaning by shifting emphasis (or, in Greek, diacritical accent).
example: "We should not speak ILL of our friends" (so it's fine to speak ill of others).
not_fallacious_when: Emphasis is legitimate when it clarifies the intended meaning.

name: Allegorical idols
definition: Using an abstraction like "the Law" or "the Church" so that the honour due to it shields the people who run it.
example: "Criticising these judges is an attack on the Law itself."
not_fallacious_when: Institutions do deserve some respect beyond their staff; the argument must still address the conduct.

name: Amphiboly
definition: Ambiguity from sentence structure rather than a single word.
example: "The police were told to stop drinking on campus after midnight."
not_fallacious_when: Ambiguous sentences are harmless when context fixes the reading.

name: Appeal to definition
definition: Using a dictionary definition as proof a term can't have another or broader meaning.
example: "The dictionary says 'theory' means a guess, so evolution is just a guess."
not_fallacious_when: Dictionaries are good evidence of common usage.

name: Bad classification
definition: Grouping things under one name though they share no important property, then generalizing about the group.
example: Lumping all "toxins" together and concluding they're all harmful at any dose.
not_fallacious_when: Rough classes can be useful starting points.

name: Category mistake
definition: Presenting facts of one logical type as if they belonged to another.
example: Asking where "the university" is after being shown every building.
not_fallacious_when: Metaphor deliberately crosses categories without inferential claims.
primary_sources: Ryle, The Concept of Mind (1949), ch. 1

name: Changing the premises
definition: In a chain of argument, proving one proposition and then building on a different one that resembles it.
example: Proving "some taxation is legitimate" and then arguing as if "this tax is legitimate" had been shown.
not_fallacious_when: Moving to a stronger premise is fine if it's separately supported.

name: Circular definition
definition: Defining a term using the term itself or a synonym.
example: "A cause is that which causes."
not_fallacious_when: Inter-defined primitives are unavoidable at some point in any system (Spinoza's Ethics starts from definitions taken as given).

name: Composition
aliases: fallacy of composition; combination (of words, Aristotle; modern mapping contested)
definition: Inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do.
example: "Every player is excellent, so the team is excellent."
not_fallacious_when: Some properties do transfer (every brick is red, so the wall is red); the question is whether this property is one of them. Note: Aristotle's "combination" concerns combining words, and its identity with the modern part/whole fallacy is disputed.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 4 166a23; ARI-RH II.24 (line 2); WHA; MIL V.vii; FIS ch. VIII; SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-RH WHA MIL FIS SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Dangling comparative
aliases: hanging comparative; incomplete comparison; faulty comparison
definition: A comparison that omits what is being compared to, or compares unlike things.
example: "Our cereal has 30% more fibre!"
not_fallacious_when: Fine when the comparison class is obvious from context.

name: Definist fallacy
definition: Defining a term in a way that makes one's position easy to defend, or (Frankena) defining one property (good) as another (pleasant).
example: "By 'evidence' I mean anything that supports my view."
not_fallacious_when: Philosophical analysis does propose definitions; the fallacy is assuming them rather than defending them.

name: Distinction without a difference
definition: Claiming two positions differ when they don't in practice, or using an empty distinction to oppose something while seeming to support it.
example: "I support a free press, just not its licentiousness" (with no criterion for the difference).
not_fallacious_when: Many fine distinctions are real and important; ask for the criterion.

name: Division
aliases: fallacy of division; division (of words, Aristotle; mapping contested)
definition: Inferring that parts have a property because the whole does.
example: "The company is rich, so each employee is rich."
not_fallacious_when: Some properties do distribute (the box is entirely inside the room, so each item in it is).
primary_sources: ARI-SE 4 166a33; ARI-RH II.24 (line 2); WHA; MIL V.vii; FIS ch. VIII; SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-RH WHA MIL FIS SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Doorman fallacy
definition: Reducing a role to its most visible task, ignoring its full value.
example: "We can replace the doorman with an automatic door."
not_fallacious_when: Some roles really are reducible; show it.

name: Equivocation
aliases: ambiguity (homonymia, Aristotle); ambiguous middle; ambiguous middle term; homonymy (Schopenhauer); fallacy of ambiguity
definition: Using a word in two senses within one argument so the conclusion seems to follow.
example: "The end of life is death; happiness is the end of life; so happiness is death."
not_fallacious_when: Deliberate wordplay is fine when no inference rides on it; terms can legitimately be extended if the shift is flagged. Pragma-dialectics: breach of the usage rule.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 4 165b30; ARI-RH II.24 (line 1b, similar words); SCH 2; WHA (semi-logical); MIL V.vii; SEP §1; PD (usage rule); WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-RH WHA MIL SCH PD SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Etymological fallacy
definition: Assuming a word's original meaning is its true or current meaning.
example: "'Decimate' means to kill one in ten, so you can't say a plague decimated the city."
not_fallacious_when: Etymology can illuminate how a concept developed and what older texts meant.

name: False equivalence
definition: Treating two things as equivalent because they share some feature, ignoring important differences.
example: "Both sides lie, so they're equally untrustworthy."
not_fallacious_when: Pointing out real shared features is fair when the differences are acknowledged.

name: Form of expression
aliases: figure of speech (figura dictionis); fallacy of the form of expression
definition: Being misled by grammatical form, treating words that look alike as the same kind of thing (an action, a quality, a substance).
example: "'Flourishing' is grammatically like 'cutting', so flourishing is something one does to things."
not_fallacious_when: Grammatical analogy is a useful heuristic when checked against meaning.

name: If-by-whiskey
definition: Answering a question with emotionally loaded terms that let both sides think you agree with them.
example: "If by whiskey you mean the devil's brew... I'm against it; if you mean the oil of conversation... I'm for it."
not_fallacious_when: Acknowledging that a word covers different things is legitimate if you then take a position on each.

name: Impostor terms
definition: Using flattering or bland names to hide the objectionable nature of a thing.
example: "Enhanced interrogation" for torture.
not_fallacious_when: Tactful language is fine when it doesn't hide relevant facts.

name: Intentional fallacy
definition: Insisting a text's meaning must be whatever its author intended.
example: "The poem can't be about grief; the author said it was about trains."
not_fallacious_when: Authorial intent is a legitimate interpretive factor, especially in law and history (a contested debate).

name: Line-drawing fallacy
aliases: continuum fallacy; fallacy of the beard; argument of the beard; heap; sorites; bald man; decision-point fallacy
definition: Arguing that because there's no sharp boundary, there's no real difference.
example: "There's no exact age when someone becomes an adult, so a 12-year-old is as mature as a 30-year-old."
not_fallacious_when: Vague boundaries can still demand arbitrary-but-reasonable cut-offs; sorites puzzles are real philosophical problems.

name: Loaded language
aliases: question-begging epithets; question-begging appellatives (Bentham); loaded words; loaded label; prejudicial language; emotive language; argument by emotive language; judgmental language; favourable naming (Schopenhauer)
definition: Using emotionally charged words that assume the conclusion.
example: "The death tax" vs "the estate tax".
not_fallacious_when: Evaluative words are fine when the evaluation has been argued for.
primary_sources: BEN IV.1; SCH 12; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: BEN SCH WIK IEP LF FF

name: Misplaced literalism
definition: Reading general, rhetorical or hyperbolic statements as if literal.
example: Treating "all men are created equal" as a claim about identical height.
not_fallacious_when: Holding people to the literal content of formal statements (contracts) is appropriate.

name: Motte-and-bailey
aliases: motte and bailey doctrine; strategic equivocation
definition: Advancing a bold claim, retreating to a modest one when challenged, then returning to the bold one.
example: Bold: "Science is just social power." Challenged: "I only mean scientists are social beings."
not_fallacious_when: Clarifying that one only meant the modest claim is fine if one then drops the bold one.

name: Obscurum per obscurius
aliases: explaining the obscure by the more obscure; failure to elucidate
definition: Defining or explaining something in terms harder to understand than the thing itself.
example: "Time is the moving image of eternity," offered as a working definition.
not_fallacious_when: Deep explanations may introduce new terms if they then pay their way.

name: Package-deal fallacy
definition: Assuming things often grouped together must always go together.
example: "If you oppose this tax you oppose public schools."
not_fallacious_when: Some things are genuinely bundled (a single bill).

name: Persuasive definition
definition: Slipping a value-laden redefinition into an argument while trading on the word's usual force.
example: "True freedom is obedience to the state."
not_fallacious_when: Stipulative and revisionary definitions are legitimate when declared openly and argued for.

name: Quoting out of context
definition: Excerpting words so their meaning is distorted.
example: A review saying "a masterpiece of tedium" is advertised as "a masterpiece".
not_fallacious_when: Partial quotation is fine if it preserves the meaning.
primary_sources: SEP related; WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Redefinition
definition: Changing what a word means when challenged, then acting as if the original claim survived.
example: "I said he was selfish; I meant selfish about money."
not_fallacious_when: Clarifying a vague term early, openly, and accepting the weaker claim is good practice.

name: Referential fallacy
aliases: name implies entity; "whatever can be thought of apart exists apart" (Mill)
definition: Assuming every word picks out a real thing, so having a name proves something exists.
example: "We have a word for 'fate', so fate must be real."
not_fallacious_when: Words often do refer; ask what the evidence is that this one does.
primary_sources: MIL V.iii.4 ("wherever there is a name, there must be a distinguishable separate entity"); WIK

name: Reification
aliases: hypostatization; misplaced concreteness (Whitehead); concretism; personification of abstractions (Mill)
definition: Treating an abstraction as a concrete thing or agent.
example: "Society made him commit the crime."
not_fallacious_when: Abstractions are useful shorthand when they can be cashed out in concrete terms.
primary_sources: Whitehead, Science and the Modern World (1925); MIL V.iii.4; WIK; IEP; LF

name: Scope fallacy
definition: Misreading which part of a sentence a word like "not", "every" or "necessarily" governs.
example: "Every concerned citizen who believes someone is a terrorist should report it; she believes there are terrorists; so she should report someone."
not_fallacious_when: Ambiguous scope is harmless when context fixes it.

name: Secundum quid (Aristotle's sense)
aliases: a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter; absolute vs qualified
definition: Taking something said in a qualified sense ("in some respect") as if said absolutely, or vice versa.
example: "An Ethiopian is white in his teeth, so he is white."
not_fallacious_when: Moving from qualified to unqualified claims is fine where the qualification is trivial.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 166b37; ARI-RH II.24 (line 8, omission of circumstances); SCH 3; SEP §2.1; WIK; IEP
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-RH SCH SEP WIK IEP

name: Suppressed correlative
definition: Redefining one of a pair of opposites so that it swallows the other.
example: "I'm not fat; I'm thinner than John."
not_fallacious_when: Relative terms can be legitimately context-dependent.

name: Sweeping classifications
definition: Ascribing to every member of a class what is true only of some.
example: "Kings are tyrants; crimes of kings."
not_fallacious_when: Generalizations about classes are fine when the "all" is warranted or the claim is about tendencies.

name: Type-token fallacy
definition: Confusing a type (a kind) with a token (an instance).
example: "The dodo is extinct; this dodo skeleton is a dodo; so this skeleton is extinct."
not_fallacious_when: Context usually fixes the reading.

name: Use-mention error
definition: Confusing a word with the thing it refers to.
example: "Chicago is a city; 'Chicago' has seven letters; so a city has seven letters."
not_fallacious_when: Self-reference in logic and linguistics deliberately exploits the distinction.

name: Vacuous truth (misuse)
definition: Making a claim that is technically true only because its subject class is empty, and implying more.
example: "No phones in this room are switched on" (there are no phones).
not_fallacious_when: Vacuous truths are legitimate in logic and mathematics.

name: Vagueness exploitation
aliases: vagueness; vague generalities (Bentham); fallacy of vague generalities
definition: Using terms too vague to test, so the claim can't be pinned down.
example: "Defend Order and the Constitution against the reformers!"
not_fallacious_when: Some vagueness is unavoidable and harmless when precision isn't needed.

name: Accident
aliases: dicto simpliciter; sweeping generalization; destroying the exception
definition: Applying a general rule to a case that is an obvious exception.
example: "Cutting people is a crime; surgeons cut people; so surgeons are criminals."
not_fallacious_when: General rules are presumptions; applying them by default is fine until an exception is shown.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 166b28; ARI-RH II.24 (line 5); WHA; SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-RH WHA SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Anthropomorphism
definition: Attributing human intentions or feelings to non-human things and reasoning from that.
example: "My car hates Mondays."
not_fallacious_when: Intentional language is a useful shorthand (Dennett's intentional stance) when not taken as evidence.

name: Baconian fallacy
definition: Thinking a historian (or inquirer) can proceed without preconceived questions, theories or hypotheses, gathering facts until the truth emerges.
example: "I just collected all the facts; I had no hypothesis."
not_fallacious_when: Open-minded data gathering is good practice; the fallacy is believing one has no framework.
primary_sources: FIS (Fischer 1970, ch. I, archive.org text); WIK

name: Begging the question
aliases: petitio principii; question-begging; subverted support (related); questionable begging
definition: Using as a premise something that assumes the conclusion or is no more acceptable than it.
example: "Smoking is deadly because it can kill you."
not_fallacious_when: Valid deductions always "contain" their conclusions in a sense; the fault is dialectical: the premise wouldn't be granted by someone who doubts the conclusion. Pragma-dialectics: breach of the starting-point rule.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 167a36; ARI-PA II.16; WHA (premises unduly assumed); MIL V.vii; SCH 6; SEP §1; PD (starting point rule); WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-PA WHA MIL SCH PD SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Circular reasoning
aliases: circulus in probando; circulus in demonstrando; vicious circle; circular argument
definition: Supporting a claim by a chain of reasons that ends with the claim itself.
example: "The book is true because it says so, and what it says is true because it's the book."
not_fallacious_when: Coherentist justification and reflective equilibrium allow mutual support among many beliefs; small circles add nothing, large webs can.

name: Complex question
aliases: loaded question; fallacy of many questions; plurium interrogationum; fallacy of presuppositions
definition: A question that presupposes something unproven, so any direct answer concedes it.
example: "Have you stopped cheating on your taxes?"
not_fallacious_when: Presupposing what both sides have actually agreed is fine.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 167b38; SCH 7 (many questions at once); FIS ch. I; SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE SCH FIS SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Denying the correlative
aliases: false alternatives to a true dichotomy
definition: Introducing alternatives where two options really are exhaustive and exclusive.
example: "Is it true or false?" "Well, it's complicated" (when it isn't).
not_fallacious_when: Questioning a supposed dichotomy is often right.

name: Double standard
definition: Judging similar cases by different standards.
example: "We'll hire men who score 70, but women need 80."
not_fallacious_when: Different treatment is fair when the cases differ in a relevant respect.

name: Fallacy of exhaustive effort
definition: Assuming that when ideal conditions can't all be met, meeting as many as possible yields the next best result.
example: "We can't have perfect competition, so let's maximise as many of its conditions as we can."
not_fallacious_when: Sometimes approximating ideal conditions does help; this has to be shown (cf. Lipsey & Lancaster's theory of the second best).

name: Fallacy of irrevocable laws
aliases: irrevocable laws; vows or promissory oaths (Bentham); dead-hand argument
definition: Treating past enactments or oaths as binding forever so present reasons can't be heard.
example: "Our founders made this law; changing it betrays them."
not_fallacious_when: Stability, trust and entrenchment have real value, argued on their own merits.

name: False dilemma
aliases: false dichotomy; black-or-white fallacy; black-and-white fallacy; bifurcation; either/or fallacy; all-or-nothing; excluded middle (misapplied); no middle ground; glaring contrast (Schopenhauer)
definition: Presenting two options as the only ones when others exist.
example: "You're either with us or against us."
not_fallacious_when: Some choices really are binary; the fallacy is in the false premise that they are.
primary_sources: SCH 13; PR III.xix (imperfect enumeration); WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: PR SCH WIK IEP LF FF

name: Goomba fallacy
definition: Treating different members' statements as if the whole group held all of them, then charging the group with inconsistency.
example: "Online, they say X and also not-X; what hypocrites."
not_fallacious_when: A group with stated official positions can be held to them.

name: Historian's fallacy
definition: Judging past decision-makers as if they had information available only later.
example: "Generals in 1914 should have known the war would last years."
not_fallacious_when: Asking what decision-makers could reasonably have known is a proper historical question.
primary_sources: FIS (Fischer 1970, pp. 209–213, per Wikipedia citation); WIK; LF

name: Historical fallacy (Dewey)
definition: Assuming a result occurred only because of a particular process that may be unrelated to it.
example: Reading the final stage of a development back into its start.
not_fallacious_when: Tracing processes is legitimate when evidence links them.
primary_sources: Dewey, "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology" (Psych. Review 3, 1896); WIK

name: Homunculus fallacy
definition: Explaining a capacity by positing an inner agent with that same capacity, leading to a regress.
example: "We see because a little viewer in the brain watches the images."
not_fallacious_when: Decomposing a capacity into simpler sub-capacities (Dennett's "discharging" homunculi) is legitimate.

name: Ideology-driven argumentation
definition: Presupposing an unargued part of one's ideology.
example: "Since the free market always works, regulation can only hurt."
not_fallacious_when: Shared premises within a community can be presupposed legitimately among those who share them.

name: Inconceivability fallacy
aliases: "whatever is inconceivable must be false" (Mill); a priori fallacy
definition: Treating our present inability to conceive something as proof it is impossible.
example: "Action at a distance is inconceivable, so gravity must work by contact."
not_fallacious_when: Logical contradictions really are impossible; conceivability can be weak evidence of possibility.

name: Inconsistency
definition: Accepting claims that cannot all be true together.
example: "I never generalize; people who generalize are hypocrites."
not_fallacious_when: Recognized tensions can be held provisionally while inquiry proceeds (paradoxes).

name: Is-ought fallacy
aliases: is-ought jump; Hume's guillotine violation; Hume's law (violation)
definition: Deriving a conclusion about what ought to be from premises only about what is.
example: "People have always eaten meat, so they ought to."
not_fallacious_when: Whether "ought" can be derived from "is" is itself contested (Searle 1964; ethical naturalists); bridging premises can make the step explicit.

name: Kettle logic
definition: Offering several defences that contradict one another.
example: "I never borrowed the kettle, it was already broken, and I gave it back undamaged."
not_fallacious_when: Arguing in the alternative is accepted legal practice when clearly framed as hypothetical ("even if").
primary_sources: Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams (1900); Jokes and their Relation to the Unconscious (1905); WIK; LF

name: Middle ground
aliases: argument to moderation; false compromise; fallacy of the mean; argumentum ad temperantiam; golden mean fallacy
definition: Assuming a compromise between two positions must be correct.
example: "Some say the earth is round, some flat; the truth is probably in between."
not_fallacious_when: Compromise is often wise in negotiation over interests; it isn't a guide to truth.

name: Mind projection fallacy
aliases: projecting one's state of knowledge onto nature
definition: Assuming a feature of one's perception or knowledge is a property of the object.
example: "Random" treated as a physical property of a coin rather than our ignorance of the outcome.
not_fallacious_when: Some properties are genuinely relational and can be described as such.
primary_sources: Jaynes (Probability Theory, 2003, and earlier papers); WIK

name: Moralistic fallacy
definition: Inferring what is the case from what ought to be the case.
example: "Men and women ought to be treated equally, so there can be no average differences between them."
not_fallacious_when: Moral premises can be evidence about what people will do (since norms shape behaviour).
primary_sources: Davis 1978 (coined; per secondary sources); WIK; LF

name: Naturalistic fallacy
definition: (Moore) Identifying goodness with a natural property such as pleasure; (popularly) deriving values from facts.
example: "Good just means what we evolved to desire."
not_fallacious_when: Ethical naturalists argue some such identities are correct a posteriori; Moore's open-question argument is contested.
primary_sources: Moore, Principia Ethica (1903), §§10–14; WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Naturalistic fallacy fallacy
definition: Rejecting every inference from facts to values just because some is-ought inferences are invalid.
example: "You can't cite suffering as a reason it's wrong; that's the naturalistic fallacy!"
not_fallacious_when: Pointing out an unbridged is-ought gap is fine; the error is treating all such inferences as invalid by form.

name: Nirvana fallacy
definition: Rejecting a realistic option because it isn't perfect.
example: "Seatbelts don't prevent all deaths, so they're pointless."
not_fallacious_when: Pointing out a cheap, better available alternative is legitimate.

name: No true Scotsman
definition: Protecting a generalization from counterexamples by redefining the group to exclude them.
example: "No true scientist doubts X." "Here's one." "Then he's not a true scientist."
not_fallacious_when: Defining group membership by a stated criterion is fine if the criterion is fixed in advance and not tailored to the counterexample.
primary_sources: Flew, Thinking About Thinking (1975); WIK; IEP; LF

name: Oversimplification
definition: Making a complex problem look much simpler than it is.
example: "The election is only about trade with Cuba."
not_fallacious_when: Models and summaries must simplify; the test is whether the omitted factors change the conclusion.

name: Political correctness fallacy
definition: Assuming groups, individuals or ideas are equal in value or truth mainly to avoid giving offense.
example: "All theories of the earth's shape deserve equal class time."
not_fallacious_when: Equal respect for persons is a sound moral principle; it doesn't imply equal truth of ideas.

name: Presentism
definition: Judging or interpreting the past by present-day ideas and values as if they were timeless.
example: "Ancient authors were stupid for not knowing germ theory."
not_fallacious_when: Moral evaluation of the past by defensible standards is legitimate if made explicit.

name: Proving too much
definition: An argument whose reasoning, if sound, would also prove things known to be false.
example: "Free will can't exist because our choices have causes" (would also rule out deliberation being meaningful in any sense).
not_fallacious_when: Showing an argument proves too much is itself a legitimate refutation technique (a reductio).

name: Psychologist's fallacy
definition: An observer assumes their own viewpoint is the subject's, or confuses their standpoint with the facts.
example: A researcher assuming a child sees the experiment as the researcher does.
not_fallacious_when: Empathic projection is a starting hypothesis to be checked.
primary_sources: James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. VII; WIK

name: Question-begging analogy
definition: An analogy that only works if the conclusion is already granted.
example: "Abortion is like murder because both kill a person."
not_fallacious_when: Analogies are fine when the shared feature is independently agreed.

name: Special pleading
definition: Applying a rule to others while exempting oneself or a favoured case without a relevant reason.
example: "Lying is wrong, but when I lie it's for a good cause."
not_fallacious_when: Exceptions are fine when a relevant difference is given (that's how rules get refined).

name: Stolen concept fallacy
definition: Using a concept while denying something it logically depends on.
example: "Reason is unreliable," argued for by reasoning.
not_fallacious_when: Self-referential critique can be legitimate as a reductio of a position (a kind of retorsion).

name: Sunk cost fallacy
definition: Continuing an endeavor because of what has already been spent rather than future costs and benefits.
example: "We've spent millions; we can't stop now."
not_fallacious_when: Past investment can be evidence of commitment or reputation costs that do matter going forward.

name: Tokenism
definition: Treating a token gesture as a substitute for the real thing.
example: "We hired one woman; the company has no gender problem."
not_fallacious_when: A first step can be meaningful if presented as such.

name: Verbal distinctions mirror nature
aliases: "differences in nature must correspond to our received distinctions" (Mill); folk classification fallacy
definition: Assuming that things we call by different names, or sort into different classes, must differ in nature and cause.
example: "Heat and motion have different names, so they must be different kinds of thing."
not_fallacious_when: Folk categories are often good starting hypotheses that track real kinds.

name: Ad hoc rescue
definition: Saving a belief from contrary evidence with an assumption whose only support is that it saves the belief.
example: "The psychic failed because sceptics' negative energy interferes."
not_fallacious_when: Auxiliary hypotheses are legitimate when independently testable (the discovery of Neptune).

name: Alleged certainty
definition: Stating a conclusion with language of certainty ("obviously", "everyone knows") instead of evidence.
example: "Everyone knows that diet doesn't matter."
not_fallacious_when: Fine when the matter really is settled and uncontroversial among the audience.

name: Amazing familiarity
definition: A claim containing information the author could not have known.
example: A "true story" reporting a lone hiker's private thoughts before he vanished.
not_fallacious_when: Reconstruction can be legitimate if labelled as such.

name: Anecdotal fallacy
aliases: argument from anecdote; anecdotal evidence; argument from anecdote or anecdotal fallacy; personal experience fallacy
definition: Treating personal stories as decisive evidence against better data.
example: "My uncle smoked and lived to 90, so smoking isn't harmful."
not_fallacious_when: Anecdotes can illustrate, generate hypotheses, or refute strict universals.
primary_sources: ARI-RH II.24 (line 4, sign or single instance); WIK; IEP; FF

name: Appeal to coincidence
definition: Writing off a result as chance when the evidence strongly suggests a systematic cause.
example: "It was just a coincidence that all the winners were the organizer's friends."
not_fallacious_when: Coincidences do happen; test against a base rate.

name: Argument from hearsay
definition: Relying on second-hand reports, losing reliability with each step.
example: "My friend's cousin heard the mayor took bribes."
not_fallacious_when: Chains of testimony can be reliable when each link is trustworthy and checkable.

name: Argument from ignorance
aliases: argumentum ad ignorantiam; appeal to ignorance; proving non-existence
definition: Concluding a claim is true because it hasn't been disproven, or false because it hasn't been proven.
example: "No one has proven ghosts don't exist, so they do."
not_fallacious_when: Absence of evidence is evidence of absence when we would expect evidence if the claim were true (a thorough search). Locke's original ad ignorantiam was a demand to "assign a better" proof.
primary_sources: LOC IV.xvii.20; SEP §2.4; Hahn & Oaksford 2007 (Psych. Review 114); WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: LOC SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Argument from incredulity
aliases: personal incredulity; divine fallacy (variant); appeal to complexity
definition: Concluding something is false (or must be supernatural) because one can't imagine how it could be true.
example: "I can't see how an eye could evolve, so it didn't."
not_fallacious_when: Mill's "whatever is inconceivable must be false" is a related a priori fallacy; but genuine inconceivability of a contradiction is a good reason.

name: Argument from repetition
aliases: argumentum ad nauseam; argumentum ad infinitum; argument by repetition; repetition
definition: Repeating a claim until objections stop, then treating silence as agreement.
example: Saying "the election was stolen" daily for months.
not_fallacious_when: Repetition is legitimate for emphasis or teaching.

name: Argument from silence
definition: Inferring a claim from the absence of mention in sources (or from an opponent's silence).
example: "No contemporary historian mentions the battle, so it never happened."
not_fallacious_when: Strong when the source would surely have mentioned it.

name: Confusing currently unexplained with unexplainable
definition: Assuming what science can't yet explain can never be explained.
example: "Science can't explain consciousness now, so it never will."
not_fallacious_when: Some problems may be principled limits (e.g. undecidability), argued as such.

name: Conspiracy theory (as argument)
definition: Explaining away missing evidence by claiming it is being hidden by conspirators.
example: "There's no evidence because they destroyed it."
not_fallacious_when: Real conspiracies happen and are uncovered with evidence.

name: Disregarding known science
definition: Making a claim that ignores well-established science weighing against it.
example: A grant proposal assuming bone colour determines strength.
not_fallacious_when: Science can be wrong; challenges should engage the evidence.

name: Fact-to-fiction fallacy
definition: Supporting a narrative with facts that don't support it.
example: Citing true crime statistics that don't show the claimed trend.
not_fallacious_when: Facts that partly support a narrative should be presented with their limits.

name: False attribution
definition: Supporting a claim by citing a source that is irrelevant, unqualified, unidentified, biased or invented.
example: "As Einstein said, 'Compound interest is the most powerful force in the universe.'" (no reliable source).
not_fallacious_when: Citing a real, checkable, relevant source is the normal way to support claims.

name: Fantasy projection
definition: Treating an emotionally charged subjective experience as objective reality and demanding others accept it.
example: "I felt a presence in the room, so there's a ghost, and you have to accept it."
not_fallacious_when: First-person reports are good evidence about the experience itself.

name: Far-fetched hypothesis
definition: Offering a bizarre explanation without ruling out ordinary ones.
example: "The crop circles must be from aliens."
not_fallacious_when: Unusual hypotheses deserve consideration once ordinary ones are tested and fail.

name: Feedback fallacy
definition: Treating an evaluation as objective without checking whether its source is disinterested.
example: Relying on a rival's critique as neutral feedback.
not_fallacious_when: Interested parties can still give accurate feedback.

name: Hasty generalization
aliases: converse accident; fallacy of insufficient statistics; insufficient sample; small sample; lonely fact (Fischer); hasty induction; faulty generalization; overgeneralization
definition: Drawing a general conclusion from too few or untypical cases.
example: "My two French friends are rude, so the French are rude."
not_fallacious_when: Small samples can justify tentative conclusions when variability is known to be low or stakes require early action. Port-Royal and Mill introduced inductive fallacies of this kind.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 166b37 (secundum quid); PR III.xix (faulty induction); MIL V.v; FIS (lonely fact; via Jenkins 2015); WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE PR MIL FIS WIK IEP LF FF

name: Hypothesis contrary to fact
definition: Presenting a confident claim about what would have happened had things been different, without adequate support.
example: "If I'd studied law, I'd be rich now."
not_fallacious_when: Counterfactual reasoning is central to causal and historical inference when grounded in evidence.

name: Imposter fallacy
definition: Claiming, without evidence, that a group's bad members are really infiltrators from outside.
example: "The violent protesters weren't really us; they were plants."
not_fallacious_when: Infiltration sometimes happens and can be shown.

name: Inflation of conflict
definition: Concluding that because experts disagree on details, nothing in the field can be known.
example: "Historians disagree about the war's causes, so we know nothing about it."
not_fallacious_when: Real deep disagreement can justify suspension of judgment on the disputed point.

name: Ipse dixit
aliases: bare assertion; proof by assertion; just because fallacy; "because I said so"
definition: Asserting a claim as true without support, relying on the speaker's say-so.
example: "It's true because I'm telling you it is."
not_fallacious_when: Testimony from a reliable witness is real evidence; first-person reports of one's own states are usually authoritative.
primary_sources: SCH 14 (proclaiming a conclusion as proven); WIK; LF; FF

name: Irrelevant proof
definition: Offering evidence that proves something other than the claim at issue.
example: Proving a document is old to show it's authentic as to content.
not_fallacious_when: Related evidence is fine if its relevance is explained.

name: Jumping to conclusions
definition: Concluding before gathering or weighing the relevant evidence.
example: "The lights are off; they must have moved away."
not_fallacious_when: Quick provisional judgments are needed in daily life; hold them loosely.

name: Limited depth
definition: "Explaining" something by naming its category instead of giving a cause.
example: "He's violent because he's a criminal."
not_fallacious_when: Category membership can be explanatory if the category carries a real mechanism.

name: Limited scope
