definition: A theory that explains only the phenomenon it was invented for and nothing else.
example: "Ghosts explain why my lights flicker" (and nothing else).
not_fallacious_when: New theories often begin narrow and earn wider scope.

name: Mal-observation
definition: Taking something to be observed when it is really an inference or misperception.
example: "I saw the sun rise" taken as observing that the sun moves.
not_fallacious_when: Most perception involves inference; trust it unless there's reason to doubt.

name: Misleading vividness
definition: Letting a few dramatic cases outweigh larger, duller statistical evidence.
example: "I saw a report of a shark attack, so swimming is too dangerous."
not_fallacious_when: Vivid cases can rightly prompt checking the statistics.

name: Missing data fallacy
definition: Refusing to admit ignorance by insisting that data we don't have would confirm the hypothesis.
example: "The records that would prove it were lost, but they'd show I'm right."
not_fallacious_when: Predicting what missing data will show is fine as a testable hypothesis.

name: Overwhelming exception
definition: A generalization so qualified that it says much less than it first seems to.
example: "All our customers are satisfied, except those who returned the product, complained, or didn't answer."
not_fallacious_when: Precise qualifications are honest when presented as such.

name: Proof surrogate
definition: Using a phrase that suggests proof ("studies show", "it's well known") without giving any.
example: "I don't need to tell a smart person like you that this is the right choice."
not_fallacious_when: Fine when the cited studies are named and checkable.

name: Pseudo-proof
definition: A verification statement that looks precise but on inspection is literally meaningless.
example: "The average family had 2.3 views on reform."
not_fallacious_when: Precise-sounding summaries are fine when operationally defined.

name: Quantum physics fallacy
definition: Invoking quantum physics to support a claim that has nothing to do with it.
example: "Quantum entanglement shows we're all connected spiritually."
not_fallacious_when: Real quantum explanations in physics, chemistry, etc.

name: Questionable premise
definition: Accepting an argument that rests on a premise you have reason to doubt.
example: Accepting "all politicians are corrupt" as a premise.
not_fallacious_when: Provisional premises are fine in hypothetical reasoning.

name: Refuting the proof, claiming the thesis
aliases: argument from fallacy; fallacy fallacy; fallacist's fallacy; argumentum ad logicam; bad reasons fallacy; refuting a faulty proof (Schopenhauer)
definition: Concluding a claim is false because an argument for it is bad.
example: "Your argument for vaccines was a non sequitur, so vaccines don't work."
not_fallacious_when: Showing an argument fails does remove that support; it is fine to say "this argument doesn't establish C".

name: Selective attention
definition: Attending only to parts of an argument and ignoring the rest.
example: Answering only the weakest of five points made.
not_fallacious_when: Focusing a reply on the central point is fine.

name: Spiritual fallacy
definition: Insisting a claim meant literally was "spiritual" after it fails literally.
example: "The prophecy did come true, spiritually."
not_fallacious_when: Some texts are meant symbolically from the start.

name: Stereotyping
definition: Assuming a generalization about a group applies to each member.
example: "She's an engineer, so she must be bad with people."
not_fallacious_when: Base rates about groups can be informative where individual information is missing (with ethical limits).

name: Suppressed evidence
aliases: cherry picking; incomplete evidence; ignoring inconvenient data; cover-up; card stacking; stacking the deck; slanting; one-sidedness; one-sided assessment; argument by half-truth; fallacy of exclusion; ignoring the counterevidence; argument by selective reading; non-observation (Mill)
definition: Presenting only the evidence that supports your case while leaving out relevant contrary evidence.
example: "Studies show the drug works" (citing two of twenty trials).
not_fallacious_when: Advocacy roles (a lawyer's brief) expect one side, provided the other side has a voice; summaries must select.
primary_sources: MIL V.iv (non-observation); WIK; IEP; LF; FF

name: Unfalsifiability
definition: Holding a claim so that no possible observation could count against it, and treating that as strength.
example: "If you don't feel the energy, that's proof your energy is blocked."
not_fallacious_when: Frameworks and definitions are not meant to be falsifiable; core theoretical commitments are tested indirectly (Lakatos, Quine).
primary_sources: Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1959; German 1934); IEP; LF

name: Weak analogy
aliases: false analogy; faulty analogy; questionable analogy; improper analogy; extended analogy; argument from false analogy
definition: Arguing from similarity when the cases are not alike in the respects that matter.
example: "Employees are like nails: you have to hit them on the head to make them work."
not_fallacious_when: Analogies are a basic and often strong form of reasoning (legal precedent, model organisms) when relevantly similar. Mill calls analogy "at best only admissible as an inconclusive presumption".
primary_sources: MIL V.v.6; FIS ch. IX; SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: MIL FIS SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Broken window fallacy
aliases: glazier's fallacy; parable of the broken window
definition: Counting the visible gains from destruction or spending while ignoring the unseen opportunity costs.
example: "The storm will be good for the economy; think of all the rebuilding."
not_fallacious_when: Spending can stimulate an economy in slack conditions (a contested macroeconomic question).
primary_sources: Bastiat, "Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas" (1850); LF

name: Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: correlation implies causation; coincidental correlation; correlation without causation
definition: Concluding A causes B because they occur together.
example: "Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, so ice cream causes drowning."
not_fallacious_when: Correlation is evidence of some causal connection (direct, reverse, or common cause) worth investigating.

name: Fallacy of the single cause
aliases: causal oversimplification; causal reductionism; oversimplified cause; insignificant cause; reductive fallacy
definition: Assuming one simple cause where several jointly contributed.
example: "The recession was caused by one bad law."
not_fallacious_when: Identifying the main or most manipulable cause is legitimate if others are acknowledged. Mill notes post hoc tends to single out one cause among many.

name: False cause
aliases: non causa pro causa; questionable cause; cause and obstacle confounded (Bentham); non-cause (Aristotle)
definition: Treating something as a cause when it isn't.
example: "Crime rose after the new mayor took office, so she caused it."
not_fallacious_when: Causal claims from good evidence (controls, mechanism, replication) are the backbone of science.
primary_sources: ARI-SE 5 167b21; ARI-PA II.17; PR III.xix; BEN IV.11; SEP §1; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: ARI-SE ARI-PA PR BEN SEP IEP LF FF

name: False effect
aliases: inferring the cause from an unestablished effect
definition: Judging a supposed cause true or false from what we know about an effect whose causal link hasn't been established.
example: "Crime dropped, so the new policing policy must be working."
not_fallacious_when: Inference from effects to causes is sound once the causal link is independently established.

name: Furtive fallacy
definition: Assuming significant events must have hidden, sinister causes.
example: "The war must have been secretly engineered by bankers."
not_fallacious_when: Hidden causes do sometimes operate and are shown by evidence.
primary_sources: FIS (Fischer 1970, ch. III; via Jenkins 2015 and Wikipedia); WIK

name: Ignoring a common cause
aliases: neglecting a common cause; common cause; third-cause fallacy; confounding
definition: Concluding A causes B when both are effects of a third factor.
example: "Kids with bigger feet read better" (age causes both).
not_fallacious_when: Once a confounder is measured and controlled, an association can be causally informative.

name: Lump of labour fallacy
definition: Assuming there is a fixed amount of work in an economy.
example: "Immigrants take a fixed number of jobs away from natives."
not_fallacious_when: In the short run, in a specific market, jobs can be constrained.

name: Magical thinking
definition: Attributing causal power to rituals, thoughts or symbols without evidence.
example: "I wore my lucky shirt and we won."
not_fallacious_when: Rituals can have real psychological effects (placebo, confidence) without the claimed causal path.

name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: post hoc; temporal sequence implies causation
definition: Concluding A caused B because B followed A.
example: "I took the remedy and my cold went away."
not_fallacious_when: Temporal order is a necessary clue to causation, and with controls can support causal inference.
primary_sources: ARI-RH II.24 (line 7); PR III.xix.3; MIL V.v.5; SEP §1; WIK; IEP; FF
source_tags: ARI-RH PR MIL SEP WIK IEP FF

name: Regression fallacy
aliases: regressive fallacy; ignoring regression to the mean
definition: Attributing a cause to what is just a return toward the average after an extreme.
example: "I yelled at the team after their worst game and they improved, so yelling works."
not_fallacious_when: An intervention may truly help; you need a control group to tell the difference.
primary_sources: MIL V.v (related remarks); IEP "Regression"; WIK; LF; FF

name: Resemblance fallacy
aliases: "conditions of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon" (Mill)
definition: Assuming causes must resemble their effects.
example: "Only a mind could produce a mind."
not_fallacious_when: Structural similarity between cause and effect can be a clue in some domains.

name: Retrospective determinism
definition: Assuming that because something happened, it was bound to happen.
example: "The empire's fall was inevitable."
not_fallacious_when: Some outcomes really were overdetermined; argue it.

name: Reverse causation
aliases: wrong direction; reversing causation; retrogressive causation (related)
definition: Mistaking the effect for the cause.
example: "People who use walking sticks fall more, so sticks cause falls."
not_fallacious_when: Feedback loops can make causation run both ways.

name: Slippery slope
aliases: domino fallacy; thin edge of the wedge; camel's nose; fallacy of distrust ("What's at the bottom?", Bentham)
definition: Claiming a first step will inevitably lead to an extreme result without showing the links are likely.
example: "If we allow same-day voting, next it'll be no voter ID, then total fraud."
not_fallacious_when: Many slopes are real: precedent, incentive and legal-reasoning chains can make later steps likely (Walton 1992; Volokh 2003).
primary_sources: BEN II.3; WAL (Slippery Slope Arguments, 1992); SEP §1; WIK; IEP; LF; FF
source_tags: BEN WAL SEP WIK IEP LF FF

name: Biased sample
aliases: unrepresentative sample; biased statistics; biased generalizing; self-selection; unrepresentative generalization
definition: Generalizing from a sample chosen in a way that doesn't reflect the whole population.
example: "Our website poll shows 90% of people love our product."
not_fallacious_when: Convenience samples can be useful for exploration or when the trait is unlikely to correlate with how the sample was chosen.

name: Curve fitting
definition: Building a model so closely to past data, noise included, that it fails on new data.
example: A 12-term polynomial that matches last year's prices exactly and then predicts nonsense.
not_fallacious_when: Fitting is legitimate with regularization, cross-validation and theory-driven constraints.

name: Ecological fallacy
definition: Inferring facts about individuals from group-level statistics.
example: "Richer states vote more for party X, so richer people vote more for party X."
not_fallacious_when: Group data can support individual-level hypotheses when individual data confirm them or models account for aggregation.

name: Exception fallacy
definition: Inferring something about a whole group from a few exceptional individuals.
example: "My grandfather smoked and lived to 95, so smoking isn't harmful for our family."
not_fallacious_when: Single cases can falsify a universal claim (one black swan).
primary_sources: engine F056 (not found in the surveyed catalogs under this name; it is used in epidemiology and research-methods texts)

name: Fake precision
aliases: false precision; misplaced precision; spurious accuracy; over-precision; specificity (IEP)
definition: Presenting numbers more precisely than the evidence allows, implying false certainty.
example: "The cloud is 5,005.6833 feet wide."
not_fallacious_when: Reporting full precision is fine in intermediate calculations or when the measurement supports it.

name: Garden of forking paths
aliases: forking paths; researcher degrees of freedom
definition: Results look significant because analysis choices were made after seeing the data, even without many explicit tests.
example: Choosing which outliers to drop after seeing that one choice gives p<0.05.
not_fallacious_when: Data-dependent analysis is acceptable when pre-registered or presented as exploratory.
primary_sources: Gelman & Loken 2013 (working paper; 2014 American Scientist); WIK

name: McNamara fallacy
definition: Deciding only on what can be measured and treating the unmeasured as unimportant or nonexistent.
example: "Body counts show we're winning the war."
not_fallacious_when: Quantification is essential; the fallacy is ignoring the qualitative factors that matter.
primary_sources: Yankelovich 1972 (coined; per secondary sources); WIK; LF

name: Multiple comparisons fallacy
aliases: p-hacking; data dredging; look-elsewhere effect; data snooping
definition: Running many tests and reporting the "significant" one as if it were the only test.
example: "We tested 20 foods; jelly beans of one colour were linked to acne (p<0.05)."
not_fallacious_when: Exploratory analysis is legitimate when labelled as such and corrected for multiplicity or confirmed on new data.

name: Observational interpretation fallacy
definition: Reading associations from observational studies as causal effects.
example: "Coffee drinkers live longer, so coffee extends life."
not_fallacious_when: Observational data can support causal claims with careful design (natural experiments, confounder control, dose-response, Bradford Hill criteria).

name: Over-extrapolation
definition: Extending a trend far beyond the range of the data.
example: "Sales doubled each year for three years, so in ten years we'll own the market."
not_fallacious_when: Short-range extrapolation with stated uncertainty is often the best available forecast.

name: Overextended outrage
definition: Treating one or a few rare outrageous cases as if they were the norm, in order to express outrage.
example: "A teacher said something awful, so schools are indoctrination camps."
not_fallacious_when: Single cases can rightly prompt outrage about that case.

name: Post-designation
definition: Announcing which correlation you were looking for only after seeing the sample.
example: After surveying patients, reporting the one symptom that happened to correlate with the drug.
not_fallacious_when: Hypothesis generation from data is fine if tested on fresh data.

name: Prodigious fallacy
definition: Treating spectacular, notorious events as if they represented ordinary conditions.
example: Writing the social history of an era from its famous scandals.
not_fallacious_when: Notorious events can be revealing when shown to be typical.

name: Simpson's paradox neglect
definition: Drawing a conclusion from pooled data when the relationship reverses within subgroups (or vice versa).
example: "Hospital A has a higher death rate," though it does better for both mild and severe cases and just treats more severe ones.
not_fallacious_when: Aggregate figures are right when the subgroups are not confounders for the question asked.

name: Spotlight fallacy
definition: Assuming the cases that get media attention represent the whole category.
example: "Air travel is dangerous; every week there's a crash story."
not_fallacious_when: Coverage can be representative when outlets sample systematically.

name: Survivorship bias
definition: Drawing conclusions only from the cases that survived some selection process, ignoring the failures.
example: "Every billionaire dropout shows college is unnecessary."
not_fallacious_when: Survivors' traits can be informative if compared against the non-survivors.

name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
definition: Drawing the target around the bullet holes: picking out a cluster after the fact and treating it as meaningful.
example: "Look, five cancer cases on this street; the cell tower must cause cancer."
not_fallacious_when: Clusters can be real signals when tested against a prior hypothesis or a proper null model.

name: Declaring a standpoint sacrosanct
aliases: sacrosanct standpoint; placing a standpoint beyond criticism
definition: Putting a view off-limits to criticism, so the other party can't challenge it.
example: "Questioning the founder's vision is not allowed here."
not_fallacious_when: Agreeing on starting points that are not up for debate in a given discussion is legitimate if mutually accepted.

name: Evasion
aliases: avoiding the question; avoiding the issue; changing the question; digression
definition: Responding without addressing the point raised.
example: Q: "Did you approve the payment?" A: "What matters is that we've reformed our procedures."
not_fallacious_when: Declining loaded or irrelevant questions is legitimate; Schopenhauer notes that evasion often signals a weak spot (stratagem 34).

name: Ex concessis argument (Lockean ad hominem)
definition: Pressing someone with consequences of their own principles or admissions. Fair as a test of consistency; becomes a trick when only an apparent inconsistency is exploited or when "you are committed to P" is passed off as "P is true".
example: "You accept that animals feel pain and that causing needless pain is wrong; so by your own lights factory farming is wrong."
not_fallacious_when: Legitimate and central to philosophical argument (Johnstone 1952 thought it the essence of philosophical argumentation); fallacious only when it pretends to establish P absolutely.
primary_sources: LOC IV.xvii.21; WHA (as ignoratio elenchi when overextended); SCH 16 (ad hominem / ex concessis trick); SEP §2.4, §2.7

name: Fallacy of metaphysical questions
definition: Trying to resolve a non-empirical question by empirical (historical) means.
example: Asking historians to settle whether history has a purpose using archives.
not_fallacious_when: Metaphysical questions are legitimate in philosophy; just don't pass them off as empirical.

name: False balance
definition: Presenting two sides as equally supported when the evidence strongly favours one.
example: A debate format pairing one climate scientist with one denier as equals.
not_fallacious_when: Hearing dissenters is valuable; weight should match the evidence.

name: Gish gallop
aliases: shotgun argumentation; proof by verbosity; argument by sheer volume
definition: Overwhelming an opponent with many weak arguments so they can't be answered in the time available.
example: Firing 20 claims in a five-minute debate segment.
not_fallacious_when: Listing many independent strong reasons is legitimate (cumulative case).

name: Having your cake
definition: Arguing so that your position is never clear, so you can back out of it.
example: "I'm not saying vaccines cause autism; I'm just asking questions."
not_fallacious_when: Exploratory discussion without a fixed position is legitimate if presented as such.

name: I'm entitled to my opinion
definition: Answering criticism by asserting a right to hold a view rather than defending it.
example: "Whatever; I'm entitled to my opinion."
not_fallacious_when: Legal and moral freedom of opinion is real; it just doesn't settle whether the opinion is correct.

name: Instance to the contrary
definition: Refuting a universal claim with a single counterexample.
example: "All swans are white." "Here's a black swan."
not_fallacious_when: This is legitimate reasoning; Schopenhauer notes how to use and resist it (check the instance is real, really falls under the claim, and really contradicts it).

name: Logic chopping
definition: Focusing on trivial technical points instead of the main issue.
example: Responding to an argument about a policy's effects only by noting a grammatical slip.
not_fallacious_when: Technical precision matters when the point is precisely where the argument turns.

name: Meaningless question
definition: Asking a question that has no rational answer as posed.
example: "What happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object?"
not_fallacious_when: Such questions can be useful for exposing inconsistent concepts.

name: Moving the goalposts
aliases: raising the bar; shifting the goalposts
definition: Demanding new or stronger evidence after the original demand is met.
example: "Show me a transitional fossil." "Now show me one between those two."
not_fallacious_when: Raising standards is fair when new information shows the original test was inadequate.

name: Presumptive proof
aliases: fallacy of the presumptive proof (Fischer); shifting of the burden of proof; misplaced burden of proof; burden-of-proof evasion (pragma-dialectics)
definition: Advancing a claim and demanding others disprove it instead of supporting it.
example: "I say the moon landing was faked; prove it wasn't."
not_fallacious_when: In some contexts the burden really lies with the other side (presumption of innocence, established consensus). Pragma-dialectics: breach of the burden-of-proof rule.
primary_sources: FIS (via Jenkins 2015); PD (burden of proof rule); IEP; LF

name: Procrastinator's argument
aliases: "Wait a little, this is not the time" (Bentham, ad socordiam)
definition: Delaying a measure with claims that the time isn't right, aiming to avoid it altogether.
example: "Now is not the time to discuss reform."
not_fallacious_when: Timing really can matter; then say when the right time is and why.

name: Rationalization
definition: Offering reasons for a view or act that are not the real reasons, because they sound better.
example: "I bought the expensive car for its safety features."
not_fallacious_when: Reconstructing better reasons for a view one holds is fine if presented as such.

name: Rejection instead of amendment
definition: Rejecting a whole proposal for a flaw that could easily be fixed by amendment.
example: "There's a typo in section 4, so the bill must be voted down."
not_fallacious_when: A flaw may be essential to a proposal; then rejection is right.

name: Self-sealing argument (closed system)
definition: Framing a position so any objection is reinterpreted as confirming it.
example: "Your resistance to my diagnosis proves you're in denial."
not_fallacious_when: Some theories legitimately predict resistance; they still need independent tests.

name: Snail's-pace argument
aliases: "One thing at a time! Not too fast!" (Bentham, ad socordiam)
definition: Insisting on slow, piecemeal change to defeat a reform without opposing it openly.
example: "Let's reform one district per decade."
not_fallacious_when: Gradualism can be prudent to manage risk.

name: Willed ignorance
aliases: wilful ignorance; argument by pigheadedness; invincible ignorance
definition: Refusing to consider evidence in order to preserve one's beliefs.
example: "I won't read that study; I know what I believe."
not_fallacious_when: Declining to re-litigate settled matters endlessly is reasonable.

name: Alphabet soup
definition: Using many acronyms and jargon to appear knowledgeable or confuse.
example: "Our KPI-driven ROI on the B2B SaaS GTM..."
not_fallacious_when: Technical vocabulary is efficient among specialists.

name: Alternative advance
definition: Offering two choices that amount to the same thing, as if they were a real choice.
example: "Would you like to sign today or tomorrow?"
not_fallacious_when: Offering real alternatives is fine.

name: Appeal to interest
aliases: argumentum ad commodum; working on the will (Schopenhauer)
definition: Winning agreement by showing that a view conflicts with the opponent's or audience's interests, rather than that it's false.
example: "If you accept this theory, your department loses funding."
not_fallacious_when: For practical decisions, interests are legitimate considerations.

name: Arguing from the opponent's false beliefs
definition: Using premises you know are false but your opponent accepts, to win agreement to a conclusion.
example: Using an opponent's misreading of a statistic to push them toward your conclusion.
not_fallacious_when: Showing that someone's own (mistaken) beliefs commit them to a conclusion is a legitimate internal critique if presented as such.

name: Argument by gibberish
definition: Using impressive but meaningless jargon so the audience assumes there must be sense in it.
example: "Consciousness is a non-local quantum holographic field of meaning."
not_fallacious_when: Hard technical writing isn't gibberish if it can be unpacked.

name: Argumentum ad auditores
definition: Raising an invalid objection that only an expert would see is invalid, so the audience sides with you.
example: A quick, technically wrong objection that gets a laugh and that takes ten minutes to refute.
not_fallacious_when: Clear public explanation is good; the fault is exploiting the audience's ignorance.

name: Asking the converse
definition: When an opponent contrarily answers "no", asking the converse so their "no" gives you what you want.
example: "Do you think this is unimportant?" to someone sure to disagree.
not_fallacious_when: None as a tactic.

name: Claiming victory despite failure
definition: Announcing that a conclusion has been proved when the answers didn't support it, relying on confidence and the audience.
example: "So, as we've established, you were wrong."
not_fallacious_when: None as a tactic; summarising a real result is fine.

name: Concealing the conclusion
definition: Getting premises admitted one by one, scattered through talk, so the opponent doesn't see where they lead.
example: A salesperson getting small yeses on unrelated-seeming points before springing the contract.
not_fallacious_when: Building agreement step by step is ordinary Socratic method when the conclusion is then openly drawn and contestable.

name: Counter-sophism
aliases: answering sophistry with sophistry; fighting fire with fire
definition: Replying to a superficial or sophistical argument with an equally sophistical counter-argument, since victory is the aim.
example: Meeting a pun-based objection with a pun-based rebuttal.
not_fallacious_when: Exposing a sophism by parody (showing the same form yields absurdity) is legitimate.

name: Deceptive sharing
definition: Sharing rare events to make them seem common, shaping perception of frequency.
example: Posting every local dog attack to suggest dog attacks are an epidemic.
not_fallacious_when: Sharing real cases is fine when accompanied by base rates.

name: Drawing the conclusion yourself
definition: Drawing the conclusion yourself instead of asking the opponent, even if a premise is missing.
example: "So, having agreed to those points, you accept my position."
not_fallacious_when: Drawing a conclusion is fine when all premises are actually conceded.

name: Feigned incompetence
aliases: ironic self-deprecation; "this passes my poor powers of comprehension" (Schopenhauer)
definition: Declaring oneself unable to understand an argument, implying it's nonsense.
example: "I'm just a simple country lawyer, but this makes no sense to me."
not_fallacious_when: Honest admission that one doesn't follow, with a request for clarification, is a virtue.

name: Forced consequences
definition: Drawing absurd or dangerous consequences from an opponent's claim by distortion, then refuting the claim.
example: "You support a carbon tax; so you want poor families to freeze."
not_fallacious_when: A real reductio (showing true implications) is legitimate.

name: Generalizing the objection
definition: When asked for a specific objection, attacking the general uncertainty of knowledge instead.
example: "Why reject this hypothesis?" "All human knowledge is fallible."
not_fallacious_when: General scepticism is a philosophical position to be argued on its own.

name: Hypnotic bait and switch
definition: Stating several uncontroversial truths in a row, then slipping in the claim you want accepted.
example: "You want a safe neighbourhood. You love your kids. You care about schools. So vote for my measure."
not_fallacious_when: Building on agreed points is the normal way to argue, if the last step actually follows.

name: Leading into paradox
definition: Steering an answerer into stating something wildly implausible, so they appear refuted.
example: Getting an answerer to "admit" that nobody ever learns anything.
not_fallacious_when: Showing that a view really implies a paradox is legitimate criticism.

name: Leading into solecism
definition: Steering the opponent into an ungrammatical expression so they appear to have erred.
example: Tripping a speaker into a grammatical slip and treating it as a refutation.
not_fallacious_when: None as an argument.

name: Making the opponent angry
definition: Provoking anger so the opponent judges badly.
example: Repeated small insults during a debate to rattle the other side.
not_fallacious_when: None as a tactic; emotional honesty about real wrongs is different.

name: Many questions at once (wide-compass questioning)
definition: Asking many sweeping questions together to hide which admission you really need.
example: A cross-examiner piling up questions so a key concession slips by.
not_fallacious_when: Comprehensive questioning is fine when each answer is given full attention.

name: Odious category
aliases: label-and-dismiss; putting it in an odious category (Schopenhauer)
definition: Getting rid of an assertion by putting it in a hated category ("That's Manichaeism", "That's socialism").
example: "That's just communism."
not_fallacious_when: Correctly classifying a view can point to known objections to that class of view.

name: Paradox trap
definition: Offering a true but unobvious proposition; if rejected, reduce the rejection to absurdity; if accepted, use it.
example: "Surely you agree some taxes are just?" used to trap either way.
not_fallacious_when: Testing someone's view with a true proposition is legitimate in inquiry.

name: Pressing the sore point
aliases: press where the opponent is angry (Schopenhauer)
definition: Pressing hardest exactly where the opponent shows anger, presuming it's their weak spot.
example: "You seem upset when I mention the audit; let's talk more about the audit."
not_fallacious_when: Noticing a defensive reaction may point to an issue worth examining fairly.

name: Provoking exaggeration
definition: Contradicting an opponent to drive them to overstate a true claim, then refuting the overstatement.
example: Pushing someone from "this policy has risks" to "this policy will destroy us," then refuting the latter.
not_fallacious_when: None as a tactic; do let people restate their own claim precisely.

name: Reducing to babbling
aliases: making the opponent babble (Aristotle); forcing repetition
definition: Constraining the answerer to repeat themselves pointlessly, so they appear foolish.
example: Pressing "double what?" questions until the answerer says "double double" (Aristotle's examples).
not_fallacious_when: Asking for clarification is legitimate.

name: Refusing a premise as question-begging
definition: Refusing to admit a premise close to the point in dispute by calling it question-begging.
example: "You're begging the question!" in reply to a fair, independent premise.
not_fallacious_when: Rightly objecting to an actual petitio is legitimate.

name: Retorsio argumenti
definition: Turning the opponent's own argument against them.
example: "He's a child, make allowances." "Precisely because he's a child, I must correct him."
not_fallacious_when: Legitimate when the turned argument really supports the other side.

name: Shoehorning
definition: Force-fitting current events into one's agenda after the fact.
example: "This storm proves my political point."
not_fallacious_when: Applying a theory to a new event is fine if the fit is tested.

name: Shuffled questioning
definition: Asking questions out of logical order so the opponent can't see the aim.
example: Asking about step 4, then 1, then 3, so the chain isn't noticed.
not_fallacious_when: Varying order is fine in genuine inquiry where no trap is intended.

name: Spin doctoring
definition: Presenting information in a misleading frame so it's interpreted as you want.
example: Calling a 20% loss "a solid foundation for future growth."
not_fallacious_when: Framing is inevitable; the fault is concealing relevant facts.

name: Spurious probability (making the weaker argument stronger)
aliases: Corax's argument; eikos reversal; making the worse argument seem better
definition: Treating a case's very improbability as making it probable ("I'm too obviously suspect to have done it").
example: "A strong man wouldn't assault anyone; everyone would suspect him," turned into a defence.
not_fallacious_when: Probabilistic reasoning about how suspicion affects behaviour can be sound if the numbers work.

name: Thought-terminating cliché
definition: A stock phrase used to end thinking on a topic.
example: "It is what it is."
not_fallacious_when: Folk sayings can encode real wisdom when offered as a reason.

name: Unasked general conclusion
definition: After getting particular cases granted, treating the general conclusion as admitted without ever asking.
example: "You agreed on all these cases, so we agree on the rule."
not_fallacious_when: Summarising agreed cases into a rule is fine if the rule is then explicitly offered for acceptance.

name: Anchoring
definition: Over-relying on the first number or piece of information encountered.
example: Estimating a house's value higher after seeing a high asking price.
not_fallacious_when: A heuristic that can be adaptive when anchors are informative.

name: Availability heuristic
definition: Judging frequency or probability by how easily examples come to mind.
example: Overrating plane crash risk after seeing crash coverage.
not_fallacious_when: A useful, often accurate shortcut; the error appears when memorability and frequency come apart.
primary_sources: IEP "Availability Heuristic"; Tversky & Kahneman 1973 (Cognitive Psychology 5); WIKB

name: Bandwagon effect
definition: Tendency to adopt beliefs or behaviours because many others do.
example: Buying a stock because everyone is buying it.
not_fallacious_when: Social learning is often rational; the fallacy is the explicit inference (see Bandwagon fallacy).

name: Belief bias
definition: Judging an argument's validity by whether you believe its conclusion.
example: Accepting an invalid syllogism because its conclusion sounds right.
not_fallacious_when: Background plausibility is relevant to whether to accept a conclusion, just not to validity.

name: Confirmation bias
definition: Tendency to seek, notice and remember information that confirms what you already believe.
example: Only reading reviews of a car you already bought.
not_fallacious_when: Not a fallacy but a tendency; it can produce cherry-picking or hasty generalization. Testing a favoured hypothesis first can be efficient if disconfirmation is also sought.
primary_sources: IEP "Confirmation Bias"; Nickerson 1998 (Review of General Psychology 2); SEP §4.4; WIKB

name: Dunning–Kruger effect
definition: Low-skill individuals overestimating their competence (as reported).
example: A novice confidently correcting experts.
not_fallacious_when: Interpretation is contested (statistical artefact debates); not a fallacy.

name: Focusing illusion
definition: Overweighting whatever aspect one is focusing on.
example: Thinking moving to California would make one much happier because of the weather.
not_fallacious_when: Focus is necessary; the fault is forgetting what lies outside it.

name: Framing effect
definition: Responding differently to the same information depending on how it is presented.
example: Preferring a treatment with "90% survival" over one with "10% mortality".
not_fallacious_when: Frames can carry real information about the speaker's recommendation.

name: Fundamental attribution error
definition: Over-attributing others' behaviour to character rather than circumstances.
example: "He was late because he's lazy" (not because of traffic).
not_fallacious_when: Character inferences are sometimes correct when behaviour is consistent across situations.
primary_sources: Ross 1977 (Advances in Exp. Social Psychology 10); WIKB

name: Halo effect
definition: Letting a good impression in one area colour judgments in unrelated areas.
example: Assuming an attractive candidate is also competent.
not_fallacious_when: Traits do sometimes correlate; the bias is over-generalizing.

name: Hindsight bias
definition: Seeing past events as having been more predictable than they were.
example: "I knew the market would crash."
not_fallacious_when: Not a fallacy; it underlies the historian's fallacy and retrospective determinism.
primary_sources: Fischhoff 1975 (JEP: Human Perception and Performance 1); WIKB

name: Hyperbolic discounting
definition: Preferring smaller rewards now over larger later rewards in a way that reverses as the delay shrinks.
example: Choosing $50 today over $100 next month, but $100 in 13 months over $50 in 12.
not_fallacious_when: Some discounting of the future is rational (uncertainty).

name: Illusory correlation
definition: Perceiving a relationship between variables, or patterns in random data, that isn't there.
example: Believing full moons cause more ER visits.
not_fallacious_when: Pattern detection is essential; the fault is not testing apparent patterns.
primary_sources: Chapman 1967 (J. Verbal Learning & Verbal Behavior 6); WIKB

name: Motivated reasoning
definition: Reasoning shaped by what one wants to conclude.
example: Scrutinizing studies that oppose one's diet far harder than those that support it.
not_fallacious_when: Not a fallacy; it is a cause of many fallacies (Mill's "moral causes" of fallacies; Thagard 2011).

name: Overconfidence
definition: Being more confident in one's judgments than their accuracy warrants.
example: Being "99% sure" of answers that are right 80% of the time.
not_fallacious_when: Confidence can be adaptive for action; calibrate it for belief.
primary_sources: Lichtenstein, Fischhoff & Phillips 1982 (in Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky eds.); WIKB

name: Rhyme-as-reason effect
definition: Judging rhyming statements as more truthful.
example: "If it doesn't fit, you must acquit."
not_fallacious_when: A memory aid; not evidence.

name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
definition: A belief or prediction that causes itself to come true, then is taken as having been correct all along.
example: A bank rumoured to fail suffers a run and fails.
not_fallacious_when: Recognizing self-fulfilling dynamics is itself good reasoning (Merton 1948).

name: Status quo bias
definition: Preferring the current state of affairs merely because it is current.
example: Keeping a default pension plan without comparing.
not_fallacious_when: Switching costs and uncertainty can make the status quo rationally preferable.
